**Analysis and forecasting of change in the marine environment a method for identifying impact of large scale offshore wind farms on marine fauna**

B. Pérez Lapeña (TU Twente) K.M. Wijnberg (TU Twente)

(We@Sea project 2006-006)

## Analysis and forecasting of change in the marine environment

_a method for identifying impact of large scale offshore wind farms on marine fauna_

B. Pérez Lapeña K.M. Wijnberg

## **Contents**

## **Preface**

This report presents an overview of the results of research project 2006-006 that was carried out within the program _PhD@Sea_ of the We@Sea project, within line 2 _Spatial Planning and Environment aspects._ The results of this research will finally be presented in a PhD thesis and in papers in peer-reviewed scientific journals. This report is a compilation of results obtained so far with an additional section discussing implications regarding identifying impact of large scale offshore wind farms on marine fauna.

The We@Sea project has identified as one of their scientific challenges, the understanding and controlling of the environmental impact of offshore wind farms. Seabirds, marine mammals, fish, and benthos are all assets that have been identified by the We@Sea project for which impacts need to be assessed and monitored. The method we developed to support ecologists in the analyses of their monitoring data could be applicable to various types of marine fauna. In our work, we have focused on the application of the method to seabird observations because We@Sea partners indicated this was where the need was highest for such methods. Also, with the focus set to seabirds, it became apparent at some point that, given the complexity of their behaviour and the characteristics of the collected datasets, geostatistical simulation was a more appropriate approach to the impact assessment problem than advancing data querying techniques for spatio-temporal data sets, as was originally believed to be the way forward.

Finally, although this report is authored by only two persons, many people contributed to the research: Suzanne Hulscher (University of Twente, PhD promoter); Jan de Leeuw and Alfred Stein (both International Institute for Geo-Information Science and Earth Observation, ITC, co-supervisors at two stages in the research); Henriet van de Veen, Fenneke Sterlini, Erik Horstman and René Buijsrogge (all University of Twente, practical and technical support);. Mardik Leopold (IMARES), Jan Tjalling van der Wal (TNO-IMARES), and Henk Kouwenhoven (NUON) provided valuable feedback in We@Sea ‘users’ meetings.

## **Summary**

As has become apparent to both the popular and scientific press, assessing and monitoring the impact of human activities on the marine environment is essential as part of a road towards sustainable development. A major concern within the We@Sea project is how to study the impact of offshore wind farms on marine fauna while the undisturbed situation is poorly understood.

From the literature it becomes apparent that marine fauna distribution patterns exhibit high spatial and temporal heterogeneity. The patterns observed at the scale of impact studies will be influenced both by local time-varying conditions prevailing at the time and location of the survey (ecological factors, physical factors, human activities), and by marine fauna distribution patterns occurring at larger scales. Generally, in offshore wind farm impact assessment studies only a limited number of dedicated localised surveys is present for the pre- and post construction situation. Assessing whether observed changes in marine fauna abundance in and near a wind farm area are indeed evidence of impact, comparing a pre and a post construction situations, therefore requires an advanced analysis approach that honours these characteristics.

In this study we have developed a method based on geostatistical simulation, to assess whether a data set on spatio-temporally varying abundance of a given species in the wind farm area and its surroundings (count data) provides evidence of impact of the wind farm on that species. The method can accommodate (a) expert knowledge on species behavior in relation to site-specific and speciesspecific biological and physical factors as well as human activities, and (b) statistical properties of the collected data over various temporal and spatial scales, including effects of varying surveying layout. Part (a) accounts for understood variation in observed species abundance between surveys, while part (b) accounts for variation in species abundance that can only be characterised in a stochastic sense. The latter characteristics can be derived from count data collected during the pre wind farm construction situation. This implies that we have worked under the assumption that characteristics of the marine environment affecting the distribution of species over the area may vary overnight, possibly resulting in a different species spatial pattern that is unrelated to the wind farm presence.

To demonstrate the applicability of the method in a real impact assessment study, the method has been applied in the case of the Egmond aan Zee offshore wind farm (OWEZ) and its possible impact on common guillemots ( _Uria aalge_ ).  It was shown that the analysis method provided a suitable and flexible framework to investigate impact, because it could accommodate special data properties inherent in the guillemot dataset (a large number of zero counts) as well as deterministic knowledge about those areas preferred by seabirds in terms of their associated probabilities of bird occurrence. Based on statistical properties of the pre-construction count data, the current level of understanding of how common guillemots respond to various dynamic physical conditions as well as the lack of coinciding monitoring data of the physical conditions at the day of survey, the collected data provided no evidence that the wind farm area had either a positive or a negative impact on common guillemots.

## **1.    Introduction**

## _**1.1 Background to the impact assessment problem**_

The North Sea provides a range of services to a variety of commercial sectors. These include fishery, shipping and port development, tourism, oil and gas extraction, and currently, wind energy production. Next to these economical services, the North Sea also provides home to diverse fauna. Monitoring the marine environment and studying the impacts of this multifunctional North Sea space is essential towards economic and ecologically sustainable development.

With respect to offshore wind farms, attempts have been made within the We@Sea project context, as well as in research related to other offshore wind farm projects, to assess the impact of offshore wind farms on the environment. Specifically, attention is paid to the monitoring of direct and indirect impacts of offshore wind farms on the organisms being part of the marine ecosystem. However, assessing such impact based on monitoring data is far from simple. One of the reasons is that the marine environment is a complex system, with many processes interacting in an interrelated and often unpredictable manner. Spatio-temporal variations in the marine environment characteristics influence the distribution of marine habitats and therefore, the observed patterns of organisms exploiting them.  For instance, a decrease in numbers of a given seabird species after wind farm construction can be viewed as an indicator of a negative impact. But the question to be addressed is whether such an observed decrease in seabird numbers can be attributed solely to the presence of the wind farm. For instance, a given seabird species may be attracted to a sea temperature front, being a proxy for good feeding conditions. The position of this front can change over time and cause displacement of birds from the wind farm area. The understanding of the spatio-temporal behaviour of the species under study and its interrelation with other marine phenomena is therefore an essential prerequisite to assess whether or not there has in fact been an impact.

Insight in marine fauna spatio-temporal behaviour is hampered by high variability occurring over different scales, turning data collection and the understanding of the resulting information into a complex task. When analysing the distribution of seabirds in a given area we encounter, for example, spatial variation that may be related to patterns in external factors such as sea temperature fronts, plus year to year variation related to population dynamics. In addition, seasonal, monthly, weekly, or daily variations may also occur, related for instance to spatio-temporal variation in food resources and daily rhythms. Therefore, a change in the marine fauna situation may be related to the wind farm presence but may also be caused by ecological, physical and other factors including other human activities in the area like commercial fishery.

Besides the abovementioned conceptual challenges, wind farm impact studies are faced with considerable challenges induced by data collection limitations. Marine data collected for impact studies tends to be scarce and patchy distributed in space and time and is affected by detection errors due to, for example, varying visibility conditions or to seabirds diving to catch prey. Another important issue is that data characteristics tend to violate traditional statistical assumptions needed for its analysis. Furthermore, data values on marine fauna abundance may be influenced by factors occurring at a different scale than the one under study. In case of migratory species this may for instance relate to changes in conditions in the breeding area located far away from the surveyed area. But also population dynamics inducing natural increases and decreases in species abundance, typically emerging at larger time scales, will affect overall species abundance.

As a consequence of the above introduced issues, marine ecologists face a real challenge on how to proceed with their impact assessment studies. This requires an analysis method capable of accommodating species behaviour in space and time as well as the characteristics of the collected data. It should also be capable of accommodating site- and species specific knowledge in a flexible manner such that it can handle increasing insight over time. The aim of this research work is to develop such a method. The analysis method should enable ecologists to assess whether collected data on given species numbers provide sufficient evidence of changes induced by a wind farm presence.

## _**1.2 Objectives**_

In this research work we aim to support ecological experts in the We@Sea project to perform a transparent analysis of multiple spatio-temporal data sets that contain (directly or indirectly) information on the impact of offshore wind farms on marine fauna. Since We@Sea partners indicated that their needs were highest for identifying impact of offshore wind farms on seabirds, the application will focus on seabirds.

The objectives of this study therefore are:

_1. To develop a method to identify whether the number of a given species observed after the construction of an offshore wind farm is evidence of changes due to a wind farm presence._

_2. To test the method with actual data collected for assessing the impact of offshore wind farms on seabirds_

The method should be flexible in order to accommodate (a) expert knowledge on species behavior in relation to site-specific and species-specific biological and physical factors as well as human activities, and (b) statistical properties of the collected data on species abundance over various temporal and spatial scales.

## _**1.3 Research questions**_

In order to reach the above mentioned objectives a series of research questions are identified:

- Which direct and indirect impacts of offshore wind farms are expected on marine fauna, and which types of methods are suitable for their assessment?

- Which ecological, physical and human induced parameters are hypothesised by experts to affect the distribution of seabirds and which are their spatio-temporal scales of variability?

- How can we incorporate the above information in an impact assessment method for analysing change in species numbers after the construction of an offshore wind farm?

- How does the developed method perform in a real impact assessment study?

- How can we use this method for improving current impact monitoring procedures?

## _**1.4 Outline of the report**_

This report is a compilation of products obtained so far ‘en route’ to a PhD thesis. Chapter two provides a literature review of methodologies and techniques allowing researchers and developers of offshore wind farms to investigate the impact of offshore wind farm projects on the marine environment with focus on seabirds. This review also appeared in the WEM-report series from University of Twente [Civil Eng. & Man Res. Reports 2008R-001/WEM-001]. Chapter three presents the method we developed for supporting impact assessment of offshore wind farms on marine fauna. It includes a demonstration case of its applicability to investigate impact on seabirds using an artificial data set. This work has been submitted to the Journal of Applied Ecology and it is currently in the peer-review process. Chapter four presents the applicability of the method in a real impact study using data collected at the Egmond aan Zee offshore wind farm (OWEZ) on common guillemots. This work has been submitted to the Journal of Sustainability Science and Management. Finally, Chapter five provides a discussion regarding the implications of the presented results for identifying impact of large scale offshore wind farms on marine fauna.

## **2. Offshore wind farm impact on the environment and seabirds in particular: a literature review**

# **Impacts of offshore wind farms on the environment**

**A review with focus on the impacts on seabirds**

**Blanca Perez Lapeña June 2008**

CE&M research report 2008R001/WEM-001 ISSN 1568-4652

## **Summary**

This report presents a documented overview of methodologies and techniques that allow researchers and developers of offshore wind farms to investigate the impact of offshore wind farm projects on the environment. The aim of this report is to list the challenge of performing such studies as the marine environment is a complex system, with a high dynamic interaction of ecosystems and physical processes influencing their spatio-temporal patterns. This is a challenge in the Environmental Impact Assessment studies including the monitoring procedures once a wind farm (or several of them) is operational.

The first section will provide some thoughts on why it is needed to evaluate impacts on the marine environment. It begins with an overview of the different uses of the Dutch North Sea Continental Shelf, with attention on offshore wind energy developments. We will look into the regulation framework for studying/protecting the environment as a consequence of human interventions. We will present different targeted ecosystems under impact studies with particular focus on seabirds.

Section two will raise the challenge of performing impact assessments of offshore wind farms on seabirds due to the complexity of the system under study. Seabirds are highly mobile organisms, presenting some predictable rhythms but responding to general and actual abiotic, biotic and human induced conditions at different (spatio-temporal) scales.

Section three will present various types of interaction between wind farm and seabirds. These interactions can be direct (e.g. collisions with wind turbines) or indirect (e.g. wind farms having an impact on fisheries which in turn has an impact on seabird distributions).

Analysis and interpretation of impacts on seabirds requires observational data and analytical techniques to process this data. Seabird survey techniques and analysis to predict seabird distributions will be described in section four.

The last two sections will be devoted to methodologies for wind farm impact assessment procedures in countries of the southern North Sea. Section five will describe studies carried out prior to the construction of a wind farm while section six will present the methods used to perform effect studies (after construction).

This report concludes by raising limitations of current approaches in assessing the impact of offshore wind farms on seabirds and the challenge of incorporating the dynamics of the influencing environment in the impact analysis. This will provide the motivation and the basis of the PhD project entitled “ _Analysis of change in the marine environment, support for environmental monitoring procedures”_ .

## **1. Offshore wind energy in the southern North Sea and the impacts on the environment: an introduction**

The Dutch North Sea Continental Shelf (NCP) has a wide range of economical uses including oil and gas exploitation, sand extraction, recreational use, fisheries and currently wind energy developments. The total area comprising the NCP extends to approximately 56000 Km[2] [3]. Large part of this area is already or will be occupied by human developments as portrayed by the figure below.

_Figure 1 different uses (economic/nature) of the North Sea [11]_

Next to the wide range of economical uses, the NCP provides home for many marine organisms. We encounter coral, common cuttlefish, Hermit crab, common shrimp, common starfish, jellyfish, cod, herring, algae, porpoise, harbour and grey seal, fulmar, guillemot, gannet and common scoter amongst others [14].

If we want to achieve sustainable development, the coexistence of these economical and nature uses of the sea requires carefully looking at their interactions.

## **1.1 Wind farms in the Netherlands**

In relation to wind farm developments, the Dutch government aims at 7500 MW installed wind capacity, of which around 1500 MW will be on land and 6000 MW at sea [40]. This means that more and more wind farms will be constructed to cope with such demand. The figure below provides an overview gathered the 29[th] October 2007 of the locations where initiatives have been presented for offshore wind energy projects (yellow polygons).

_Figure 2 overview of initiatives for offshore wind energy developments in the NCP represented as yellow polygons [32]_

Policies are also developed and applied in the Dutch continental shelf in relation to other marine economical uses. For example, the Dutch Fish Product Board is responsible, together with the government, to comply with the national and European fishery agreements [11].

Another important policy refers to the environment. Policy frameworks such as the Integrated Management Plan 2015 of the Ministry of Transport, Public Works and Water Management, the Water Directive, the Bird and Habitat Directive, and the Marine Strategy focus on the coexistence of a healthy environment with economically profitable human activities [4]. Moreover, the ecological network in the European Union territory, Natura 2000, has designated Special Protection Areas for birds and Special Areas of Conservation for other species and habitats aiming at reducing habitat degradation and the decrease of species biodiversity [2].

Avoiding conflicts amongst all the economic and nature functions of the NCP, requires careful spatial planning [21]. Despite of the usefulness of the tools for coordinating these functions, still some of the sectors may experience conflicts. For example, fishing activities will experience a reduction of marine space due to wind farm construction as the coexistence with other functions will no longer be possible. This is because fishing is forbidden in the wind farm area plus a safety zone of 500 meters around it [12].

To comply with these policies, legal instruments have been developed. For offshore wind farms and the environment, legal instruments such as Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) have to be applied. This is a requirement for the appraisal of a proposed wind farm project.

## **1.2 Environmental legal instruments for offshore energy developments**

Legislation applicable to offshore wind energy developments requires a Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) for national wind farm projects. For single projects likely to have impacts on the environment an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is required [13].

Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) is defined as the “assessment of the effects of certain plans and programs on the environment (Directive 01/42 EC), meanwhile adopted and transformed into national law in the participating countries” [5].

Within the Netherlands these instruments have been applied, for instance, to define areas with special ecological values [28]. This type of studies will be further described in section 5.1.

Environmental impact assessment (EIA) is a process of evaluating the expected environmental impacts (both beneficial and adverse) of a proposed project [50]. In the Netherlands, the Minister of Transport, Public Works and Water Management published a license system in 2004, under the Public Work Management Act (Wbr) law. The Wbr policy rules describe the requirements that a plan for an offshore wind farm must satisfy in order to obtain a building permit [39].  One of the requirements is an environmental impact assessment. The procedure for application of a license is summarized as follows:

_Figure 3 Licence application procedure. Adapted from [49]_

In order to compile an EIA document, knowledge is needed on how wind farms influence the various aspects of the marine environment. This knowledge should provide the basis for interpreting and understanding the consequences of a project implementation. In the marine environment, this may prove difficult as it is a complex system with many types of organisms and phenomena interacting in a complex (and many times, unpredictable) manner.

## **1.3 Impacts of offshore wind farms on marine fauna**

In the context of EIA, the direct and indirect effects of the project need to be identified, described, and assessed. This requires knowledge on which elements of the marine environment are affected by the expected impacts of offshore wind farms, and which of these elements must be considered as protected assets in the environmental assessment [22]. Other than these studies, in the EIA procedure a monitoring program has to be laid down, with careful consideration on identifying measurable outputs. For instance in the Netherlands, considered protected assets include, amongst others, seabirds (resting birds and migratory birds), marine mammals, fish, and benthos [22]. The expected impacts are summarized in the table below.

_Table 1 Expected impacts for some identified protected assets [22]_

|Resting and breeding birds|Disturbance, displacement, barriers of movement orcollision of seabirds due to construction and operationof turbines|
|---|---|
|Migrating birds|Collision or diversion of migrating birds due toconstruction activities and operation of turbines|
|Marine mammals|Damage to or displacement of marine mammals dueto construction and operational noise|
|Fish|Damage to fish by sediment dispersion, vibration, orelectromagnetic fields and changes in fish occurrenceby introduction of fish habitats (artificial hardsubstrates)|
|Benthos|Damage and/or loss of benthic communities throughover building, sediment exchange by introduction ofhard substrates|

In the case of seabirds, _disturbance_ can be due to the increased human activity in the wind farm vicinity or simply by the presence/noise of the wind turbines themselves [10].  Such disturbances may have as a consequence the _displacement_ from suitable habitat areas, including their main feeding grounds [13]. This displacement may produce a conflict when other alternative suitable areas are not able to accommodate the displaced birds [25]. It is also considered that wind farms may become _barriers_ to seabird’s movement. This may cause bird flocks to fly around the wind farm [8], representing a local barrier of otherwise connected feeding and roosting flights or a barrier in migratory flights. This will depend on the species, the size on the wind farm, spacing of turbines, the amount of displacement of flying birds and their ability to compensate for their energy use [13]. Bird _collisions_ with offshore turbines is an important issue as the impact of such additional mortality may have high impacts at the population level (e.g. in susceptible species) [25].

In assessing such impacts on seabirds it is very important to consider cumulative impacts when several wind farms are taken into account. For instance, building several wind farms would mean an increase in flight distance causing a negative impact which would not have occurred if a single wind farm was taken in isolation [5].

Apart from the investigation of the abovementioned impacts, detailed knowledge on spatial and temporal trends in seabird distribution has been identified as part of the EIA. Although knowledge at

a larger scale may not be really helpful when looking at the cause of the potential effects at more localized areas (e.g. in an offshore wind farm), knowledge of these spatio-temporal trends at a larger scale is important to put local findings into context [7].

## **2. Factors affecting seabird presence**

In order to assess the impacts of offshore wind farms on seabirds, knowledge of the seabird species’ spatio-temporal variability is required to understand if changes in their spatio-temporal pattern may have been caused by the placement of a wind farm.

Understanding the distribution patterns of seabirds is challenging as the actual pattern is the result of a combination of different sources of variation occurring at different spatial and temporal scales.

## **2.1 Sources and scales of variability**

The observed species distribution patterns are the result of several sources of variation.  These include, amongst others: changes in population sizes, rhythms in the species cycle, distance to breeding colonies, meteorological conditions, water temperature, salinity, turbidity, prey distribution, and fishing activities. Moreover, these sources of variation take place at different spatial and temporal scales.

Fluctuations in population sizes over time can explain increases or declines in the species numbers observed. For example, variations in Great Cormorant _Phalacrocorax carbo_ population numbers in Dutch waters have been observed with an increase over the last years [47]. In the coastal waters this has been due to the establishment of two breeding colonies in Noord-Holland [27].

Seabird species visit different locations at different times during the year. In Dutch waters we encounter species such as Black-legged Kittiwakes during the winter season[1] as breeding colonies (such as Helgoland) are located in other countries (such as Germany) [27].  The location of these colonies depends on the availability of food in the species foraging range. The species spatial distribution may also change in time as a function of the habitat characteristics in the breeding colonies [44]. Moreover, these species may show different uses of the feeding area (near the colony) at different times of the day [30].

Abiotic and biotic factors also have a high influence on seabird patterns. Seabird species are influenced by meteorological conditions [27], affecting their occurrence numbers at a given place and time. At broader scales, offshore species such as shear-waters and storm petrels can occur in the near Dutch shore waters when low air pressure areas are moving over Scotland and generate northwesterly winds [27]. For species such as wintering guillemots resting at the sea surface, it has been estimated that by the influence of actual winds, they can experiment a drift of 15 km to 68 km each day [38].

Other abiotic factors affecting seabird distribution include salinity, water depth and water transparency. Garthe [15] studied the influence of these factors, together with distance to colony, to several species in the south-eastern North Sea. Results of their analysis showed that, for example,

> 1 In this report, seasons will refer to periods within the year that are important for the species. Table 2 in section 4.2.2 provides some examples

Fulmars ́ observational data was correlated with areas of high salinity, large water depth and high transparency.

Information of these explanatory variables can be used to delineate broad scale water masses as a whole and analyze their correlation with seabird numbers. In the previous example, the Central North Sea water mass was associated with high values of salinity, water depth and water transparency and was correlated with high numbers of Fulmars [15] _._ Markones [30] analyzed the relationship of several species to two different water masses in the German Bight, the _Continental coastal_ water mass (low salinity and high turbidity) and the _Central North Sea_ water mass (high salinity and high transparency).   These were derived by means of principal component analysis combining information on sea surface salinity, water depth, water transparency, vertical and horizontal temperature gradients, and vertical and horizontal salinity gradients amongst others. Results from correlation tests between the obtained principal components and seabird observations indicated a preference by different species to the different water masses.  She also looked at the species relationships to small scale hydrographic features, more spatially variable and less persistent structures. This was the case for the Elbe River plume (with varying location, spatial extent and strength due to wind and tides) with which Black-legged Kittiwakes were significantly positive correlated [30].

In the Netherlands, Poot et al. [38] also investigated the relationship of seabird species (wintering auks: Guillemots and Razobills) with water masses and their transition zones. The positions of the boundaries of these water masses were delineated by using thresholds in salinity values (measured at 6 meters depth over the study area): _continental coastal water_ (salinity less than 34 ppt, parts per million), _channel water_ (salinity more than 34.75 ppt), and _English coastal water_ (salinity less than 34.25 ppt). Seabird counts (each count covering on average 1,4 km[2] ) were assigned to each of the water masses and statistical tests were carried out to determine whether Guillemots and Razobills occurred in each of the water masses and transition zones equally. Based on the analysis of surveys from the second to the fifth of December 2002, it was concluded that a correlation of these species to different water masses was unlikely. A similar type of analysis was used to relate seabird occurrence with water turbidity. Turbidity measures (by means of Secchi disk) were assigned to several classes using threshold values. Low turbidity areas were considered those with 0-2 FTU (Formazin Turbidity Unit), medium turbid areas those with 2-4 FTU, and high turbid areas with 4-6 FTU. Again, seabird observations were assigned to the different areas and statistical tests were carried out to assess whether the species preferred turbid/non-turbid waters. The analysis conclusions pointed out to a preference of both species to turbid waters (contrary to the expectations for being visual hunting species) and high numbers of these species occurred at the Frisian Front which, at the time of the survey, was located in the Channel water [38].

The role of water masses determining species distributions is also dependent on the different prey types they contain. As discussed in [20], prey availability may determine whether a given water mass will support certain seabird species. In his work, physical processes within water masses affecting the distribution of zooplankton species are reviewed. He provides examples such as pycnoclines and/or internal waves determining the availability of prey (e.g. zooplankton) for planktivorous species (such as _least auklets_ ), explaining the species distribution.

Other source of variation for some piscivorous species includes human activities such as fishing. Scavenger species (e.g. Herring and Lesser Black-backed Gulls) are known for scavenging behind active fishing vessels [6]. For this association to hold, food availability of “natural prey” needs to be present in the vicinity of these trawlers [38].

## **3. A review of processes responsible for the wind farm – seabird interaction**

We can consider different types of interaction when it comes to offshore wind farms and seabirds. Some of the interactions may be direct ones (such as collision) while others may interact with seabird species in an indirect way (e.g. changes by the wind farm in marine processes or in other human activities that in turn affect seabird presence).

## **3.1 Direct impact of wind farms**

In this section we consider two direct impacts, that is, collision with wind turbines and the attraction of seabirds to the wind farm area for resting purposes.

Collisions of seabirds are expected to be with the rotors and hubs of the wind turbines. When the location of the wind farm is in a migratory path or the area is used by specific seabird species, the collision risk will be higher [10]. Moreover, weather conditions may influence the risk level for such collisions. For example, species under strong winds may be pushed towards the wind farm area. In bad visibility conditions, such as fog, birds may be attracted to the illuminated offshore structures, causing collisions with the hubs or rotors [18].

On the other hand, positive impacts of wind farms with seabirds can also be expected. For example, different species may be attracted to the wind farm area. Studies such as [35] have concluded that species like Cormorants may use the erected turbines as resting structures.

## **3.2 Impact of wind farms on the bio-physical environment**

The impact of offshore wind farms on seabirds can be also seen in an indirect way. Wind turbines may change the regimes governing the wind farm location area. Examples include changes in wind conditions and physical processes such as change in currents and sedimentation [10].

Rotation of the blades creates a vortex, and may push birds towards the water with the danger of dawning [13]. Vibration of the wind turbines may influence the distribution of fish, which in turn can influence seabird species depending on this food source [10]. Due to construction of the wind park and the placement of cables, sedimentation processes may be altered. Turbidity levels may increase, which may in turn affect the feeding capabilities of visual hunting seabird species [1].

## **3.3 Impact of wind farms on other human activities**

Offshore wind farms will also produce an impact to other human activities. For example, fishery activities are forbidden within the wind farm area [23] and a buffer around it (of about 500 meters) [12]. This may affect how seabirds behave in the wind farm area. Seabird species known as being scavengers may make less use of the wind farm area as these sources of food may no longer be there.

Another impact for seabirds in relation to human activities is the risk of seabird mortality whenever vessel accidents with the wind farm structures take place [31]. This may have as a consequence oil

spills which can cause seabird death (e.g. by affecting body parts such as feathers or by the ingestion of oil) [46].

A further impact of fishing activities is the change in food resources within the wind farm area. As stated, trawling is no longer allowed and this may cause an increase of fish numbers. This may have a positive impact on seabird species that depend on this type of resources [10].

## **4. Mapping seabird distribution**

In order to understand seabird patterns and analyse the interactions of seabirds and offshore wind farms, experts rely on observational data of seabirds (and the processes affecting their distribution) together with analysis techniques for data interpretation.

Survey techniques at sea can be divided into two groups depending on the platform used to perform the surveys. In the following section we will briefly review two of these techniques, followed by an example of two datasets derived from those surveys. As sampling in the marine environment may be limited to describe important seabird patterns, we will review interpolation techniques able to predict seabird densities at unsampled locations.

## **4.1 Seabird survey techniques**

Survey methods for collecting data on seabird numbers consist of ship- and airborne-based methods. Ship-based techniques make use of a strip-transect methodology as described by Tasker et al. [45]. Within this methodology, birds are counted over transects of 300 meters (bands) wide, perpendicular to the ship track line, and at a recommended time interval of 5 minutes. In order to correct for missing birds, this methodology has been modified to subdivide each band into narrower blocks (050 meters away from the boat, 50-100 meters, 100-200 meters, and 200-300 meters) [24]. Frequency distributions of birds observed in these different distance intervals are used to obtain the number of birds possibly missed at the furthest distance [7]. Other important factors affecting the detection of birds include bird size, color, behavior, weather, and observer ability [45].

Ship-based methods allow for a detailed collection of data in the surveyed area under different weather conditions, although the extension covered by these surveys tends to be small. Moreover, ship-based surveys allow the collection of seabird behavior information and the simultaneous registration of environmental characteristics governing the species observations (e.g. water salinity and temperature) [7].

In airborne survey methods, collection of seabird data is performed from an airplane. Two observers are located at each side of the plane and within a certain distance from the plane track line (e.g. 100 meters) they record the species, number, behaviour, and time on a dictaphone [7]. Airborne survey methods provide a higher coverage during the same amount of time but they are restricted to operate during good weather conditions [7] and, over vast areas, these may cover only longitudinal transects (e.g. airborne-surveys from the seabird monitoring program here in the Netherlands cover approximately 0.5% of the extension of the Dutch continental shelf [37]). Moreover, the ability to identify and count species from an airplane is more difficult as it depends on the conditions of the sea such as the sea state and water color characteristics (e.g. it may be difficult to identify birds from the air due to the low contrast of a bird with the background sea).

One example of the uncertainties in the data induced by the survey method employed is presented in the figures below [26]. Both figures reflect the aggregated number of Fulmars for the species season of August/September. Figure 4(a) is based on ship-based counts (collected in the European Seabirds At Sea database) while in figure 4(b) the survey was carried out from a plane (collected in the longterm seabird monitoring program by RIKZ). Fulmars are pelagic species but under distant adverse weather conditions they may be displaced to more nearshore waters [27]. ## **4.2 Available transect datasets**

In this section, we examine two example datasets obtained from the two survey techniques above described. The first one has been obtained as from the Dutch seabird monitoring program and makes use of airborne survey techniques. The second dataset has been collected by ship-based survey techniques. Data collection was carried out before the construction of the two Dutch wind farms NSW and Q7 and provides the basis for the baseline studies to analyze and monitor the impact the offshore wind farms on resting seabirds.

## **4.2.1 Long-term seabird monitoring dataset**

The RWS National Institute for Coastal and Marine Management (RWS RIKZ) is monitoring seabird numbers in the Dutch Continental Shelf. The monitoring program started in 1989 and the surveys are carried out on a bi-monthly basis from an airplane.

Seasons for which flights are carried out are defined based on the following periods in the year: _season 1 = August/September, season 2 = October/November, season 3 = December/January, season 4 = February/March, season 5 = April/May, and season 6 = June/July_ .

On average, during each season the sampled area comprises 280 Km[2] . Considering that the NCP has an extension of approximately 56000 Km[2] , the surveyed area corresponds to 0.5% of the NCP area [37].

Observers are located at both sides of the plane and they count bird species during periods ranging from approximately one to two minutes (this corresponds to approximately 3km and 6kms respectively) and over a transect width of around 150 meters.

## **5. A priori impact assessment of offshore wind farms on seabirds**

As reviewed in section 1.2, impact studies prior to the construction of a wind farm have to be conducted. Studies under this umbrella aim at:

- identifying areas holding large number of seabird species and thus, excluding those as potential wind farm locations,

- analyzing vulnerability of seabird species to offshore wind farms and thus, excluding wind farm construction in sensitive areas,

- assessing potential impact on population size prior to the construction of a wind farm,

- setting the reference situation to which to compare the characteristics of the environment after the construction of the wind farm, and

- studying whether current seabird survey methods allow for changes in seabird numbers to be detected when comparing baseline data to post-construction data.

The following sections review some of these studies, together with their methods and techniques that have been carried out in countries bordering the southern North Sea.

## **5.1 Study to delineate high seabird density areas**

In the work described in [17] a technique was presented to identify those areas that should be protected because they hold large numbers of important seabird species. Observational count data collected between 1986 and 2002 (by means of ship-based and aerial surveys) was used in the analysis. The number of individuals, aggregated per seasons in the year and over the survey years, was used to generate species density maps using Ordinary kriging (spatial interpolation technique). Contour lines connecting locations with the same seabird density were drawn and the gradient of bird density change in space was calculated. The contour located outside the strongest gradient was used as the boundary of a species high concentrated area. Combining the maps with information on the concentrations per different species, a potential Special Protection Area (SPA) was designated.

## **5.2 Index for bird-presence dependent sensitivity to offshore wind farms**

Garthe et al. [16] developed an index to provide information of the areas that may be less suitable for locating wind farms based on seabird species occurrence and their sensitivity to these type of developments. It is based on the species-specific sensitivity index (SSI) which values refer to the species response to wind farms in relation to nine different factors: flight maneuverability (a), flight altitude (b), percentage of time flying (c), nocturnal flight activity (d), disturbance by ship and helicopter traffic (e), flexibility in habitat use (f), biogeographical population size (g), adult survival rate (h), and European threat and conservation status (i). Species were given scores to these factors. The scores ranged from 1 (low vulnerability) to 5 (high vulnerability). Which scores to assign was based on existing data for certain factors, while for others expert opinion was used to decide which scores to assign. The scores were then averaged within groups (a-d: flight behaviour; e-f: general behaviour; g-i: status) and multiplied by each other to obtain the SSI.

## **5.3 Study for assessing potential impact on seabird population size**

In order to assess the impacts of offshore wind farms on seabird population size, analysis like the one described in [9] were carried out. Provided that there is evidence from other projects (e.g. Denmark) of which species are sensitive to wind farms (either by risk of collision or by being displaced from otherwise suitable feeding grounds in the area), the percentage of the national species population affected was computed. Areas in which wind farm developments had been approved were delineated (in this study a total of seven containing one or more wind farms) and they were assigned seabird densities for the four seasons during the year cycle. According to the Ramsar Convention, a given area is important for a species if the area holds the occurrence of 1% of the national population size [28]. To estimate this proportion in the wind farm area, seabird observed densities were transformed into seabird counts based on the area occupied by the wind farm. This provided an estimation of the population size proportion of bird species potentially displaced. The resulting percentages were provided per species and season and aggregated by the total of approved wind farms [9].

## **5.4 Study to describe seabird distribution prior to wind farm construction**

In the Netherlands, baseline studies have been carried out prior to the construction of the NSW and Q7 wind farms [27]. Describing the pre-construction situation started by generating continuous surfaces of seabird densities, using the analysis techniques described in section 4.3. Moreover, in

order to better understand seabird use of the wind farm locations and the area surrounding them further analysis were carried out.

To estimate the selection of the wind farm area by seabird species, an extended model was derived. This was done by adding an extra parameter to equation 4.4 to account for the variation explained by the location of the count (inside or outside the wind farm area). This location “effect” was modeled as follows:

_log(expecte dcount)_ = _log(Observ edArea)_ + _S(Distance)_ + _S(Y - Field)_ + _v * (NSWorQ7)_ (5.3)

where _v_ is a regression coefficient and _NSWorQ7_ was substituted by 1 when the seabird count was recorded in the wind farm NSW (or Q7) and otherwise by 0. The significance of this extra term was tested by an F-statistic.

Using equation 4.4 and equation 5.3, it was calculated the ratio between the seabird density in the two wind farms and the seabird density from the model without the effect of location (general pattern).

The conclusion of this analysis was that there were no deviations in the patterns within the NSW and Q7 when compared to the general pattern (equation 4.4). The approach to assess if the wind farms have an impact on seabirds will then be to carry out the same type of analysis using the data for the post-construction situation ( _t1_ ) and assess again the deviations from the general pattern. If deviations are found, it will be concluded that the wind farm had an impact.

In order to put the observed results into context, species counts from the RIKZ monitoring program (described in section 4.2.1) for the years 1991-2002 were selected within two regions of the study area (considered as offshore and nearshore areas) which boundary was the 20 meter isobath. Plots were generated with information on the average bird densities per RIKZ season (section 4.2.1), year and area (nearshore/offshore). Densities were computed by adding all the observation counts and dividing it by the total surveyed area [27].

## **5.5 Study to detect change in seabird numbers**

In order to be able to evaluate if a given reduction in the number of seabirds in an area would be detectable by a seabird monitoring program, Maclean et al. [29] applied power analysis[2] to airbornebased monitoring data for 4 different species in three areas of the UK waters. The framework for the application of power analysis was to evaluate the frequency and timing of airborne survey data needed to detect pre-determined changes in seabird numbers at a given significance level.

A generalized linear model was fitted to observed count data during seasons of the year. The parameter estimates of the model served to calculate the expected mean count of birds for each season and year combination. To simulate data from the pre-construction situation, random counts for each season and year were drawn from a Negative Binomial distribution with the mean and the variance computed by the generalized linear model analysis. To simulate post-construction data, the previous mean and variance was adjusted by pre-defined declines (e.g. 50%) and random counts were also drawn from the distribution. Then, statistically tests were carried out to see if the declines could be detected. This procedure was applied many times and the statistical power (probability of detecting a pre-defined decline) was computed as the proportion of times that the decline could be tested as being significantly different than zero. Power analysis was also carried out by incorporating other environmental explanatory variables in the generalized linear model, aiming at reducing unexplained variability in the count data [29].

## **6. Posteriori impact assessment of offshore wind farms on seabirds**

Assessing whether a human activity (e.g. wind farm) has altered the environment (e.g. seabird numbers in the impact area) needs analytical tools and designs that will be able to detect change once the human activity has taken place [41]. Most of these techniques fall within the BACI framework (before-after-control-impact design). In brief, BACI designs make use of data from two types of area (impact and control areas) during a period of time before an impact takes place as well as after [42]. Control areas are chosen as having presumably similar characteristics as the impacted area. Analysis are then carried out to identify whether changes in the mean values (e.g. in seabird numbers) before and after the impact can be associated to the human activity [41] rather than to natural variability [19].

There exist different BACI designs each of them having pros and cons. For a review of the different designs, the reader is directed to the following references [43], [19], [41], and [42].

One example following the BACI approach is described in [35]. In their work, the area where the wind farm was to be constructed was surveyed during the so called baseline studies. The same area was surveyed again after the wind farm was constructed. Moreover, due to the large spatio-temporal variability of seabird behaviour, a control area (with similar characteristics as the area studied for impact) was defined. This total area was surveyed during the baseline and monitoring studies and served as a reference for comparing seabird numbers.

In the area studied for impact, airborne surveys were carried out during the pre-construction (around 16 surveys over 3 years) and the post-construction (around 15 surveys over 4 years) of the wind farm (e.g. Horns Rev). Based on these surveys, GIS layers were created containing species bird counts and survey effort on a 2x2 km grid.

> 2 Power analysis is an analytical technique used to determine the probability of detecting a specified difference in numbers when one in fact exists [29].

Based on the aggregated data over the 16 pre-construction surveys, the preference of the species for different zones: i) the wind farm area, ii) an area of 2 kms around it and iii) an area between 2 and 4 kms around it was computed using the Jacobs selectivity index ( _D_ ).

where _r_ is the proportion of the number of a bird species within the impact area in relation to the numbers in the total surveyed area and _p_ is the proportion of survey effort within the impact area in relation to the effort in the total surveyed area.

This index expresses the preference of the bird species for the specified zone and ranges from -1 (all birds are outside the area) to +1 (all birds are inside the area).

One-sample χ[2] tests were performed to test significant differences between the observed number of birds in the different zones and the numbers of birds expected. The expected number of birds was calculated using the proportion of the transect length in the area of interest to the transect length in the total area surveyed [35].

The same procedure was carried out to analyze the post-construction survey data. A comparison between the _D_ -values of the pre- and post-construction was used to determine changes in the bird species use of the different zones [35].

Student t-tests were also performed with the data prior and after the construction of the wind farm. This served to analyze if mean seabird densities (in the work this is approximated by bird encounter rate corrected for survey effort) in the three different zones, and the control area (4kms away from the farm were no effects where expected) differed significantly for the pre- and post-construction period [35].

In the work, they also described whether the pre- and post- construction cumulative frequency distributions of bird numbers at intervals of 500 meters from the wind farm were significantly different. The distributions were obtained by taking the distance from each observation to the nearest turbine and grouping the numbers in 500 meters distance intervals. Both distributions were compared for statistical differences by a Kolmogorov-Smirnov Two-sample test [35].

Furthermore, it was also assessed the minimum detectable change in seabird numbers within the wind farm area that would be statistically significant when comparing the pre- and post-construction situations. A two-sample χ[2 ] test was used for this purpose. Seabird numbers from the year baseline surveys where tested against a hypothetical decline of e.g. 10%, 25%, and 50% of these numbers to assess when this artificial reductions would be statistically significant [36].

## **7. Discussion and conclusions**

This report provides the legal framework for environmental impact assessments of offshore wind farms on seabirds together with a summary of seabird related studies carried out in different countries of the southern North Sea. To capture the complexity of understanding and analyzing seabird distribution patterns, we looked at examples of the natural variability characteristics for certain species (section 2.1). This represents a challenge when performing environmental studies. For instance, in the case of impact studies of offshore wind farms on seabirds, a pre-construction situation (t0) for the species has to be described. This pre-construction situation will be later on

compared to the post-construction situation (t1) to determine if deviations from the t0 pattern can be attributed to the wind farm. But which t0 realization should be taken as such reference?

In the effect studies described in section 6, the expected value for the number of birds in the wind farm area is computed by the proportion of the survey effort in the wind farm area in relation to the effort in the total area studied for impact. We have seen that seabirds may pick in areas with certain environmental/human induced characteristics (e.g. in a tidal front or near active fishing vessels) and not accounting for this variation may bias the conclusion that a species avoids the wind farm area. This point is better raised by an example. Let us suppose that a species uses the wind farm area during the pre-construction surveys as depicted in the figure 16(a). The figure presents the wind farm area as a black polygon and the factors such as fishing vessels, suitable feeding grounds, and distance to colony affecting the numbers of birds observed at a given moment in time. In this case, the computed selectivity index ( _D1_ ) may be high. If we compute the same index for the post-construction situation (figure 16(b)) and compare it to _D1_ we may conclude that the wind farm had an effect on the displacement of seabird species.

_Figure 16 (a) example setting for the t0 situation and (b) example setting for the t1 situation_

In order to be able accept an avoidance conclusion, the values of the variables explaining the variation of a certain species pattern should had been the same.

The same applies for the modeling procedure described in Leopold et al. [27]. The reference situation (t0) has been described as one, when in fact many t0 situations really exist. Some of the variation in the collected data has been qualitative described (e.g. the relation of high numbers of gull species associated to fishing vessels) but has not been quantitatively accounted for in the modeling procedures. This has resulted in a high amount of variance in the seabird data. It has been estimated that only changes in the order of 50-100% would be found in a (statistical) significant sense if t0 and t1 seabird densities would be compared [27].

In fact, a common conclusion by the different studies was the need to include explanatory variables in the modeling procedures. Given the response of seabirds to the marine characteristics at the moment of the survey, such explanatory variables should be included in a dynamic fashion. The work performed in [29] considered the type of variation due to environmental factors. The limitation in that case was that the spatial explanatory variables were taken as static (not changing over time such as water depth) and could not be used to account for temporal variation in species numbers. In

the study carried out by Poot et al. [38], an explanatory dynamic factor such as salinity was included in the modeling procedure, although model outcomes did not well capture important marine features affecting seabird patterns.

Other than the external factors affecting the observed numbers at a given location and a given time, there exists a ‘history’ on the spatio-temporal seabird pattern. And this operates at different spatial and temporal scales. For instance, it has been realized that seabird concentrations have undertaken a shift from north to south in the Dutch continental shelf. In addition, seabird population sizes for certain species may have fluctuated during the years, and the location of breeding colonies may have changed over time (refer to section 2.1). All this information may generate variability in the species patterns that needs to be accounted for when assessing possible deviations in the post-construction wind farm situation.

In summary, in order to be able to assess the effects of an offshore wind farm on seabirds, information on the species “history”, and actual dynamic factors affecting the observed numbers at the moment of the surveys should be taken into account when analyzing the post-construction situation ( _t1_ ).
